title: Methods Checkpoint
intro: You can split a program into named pieces now: methods, parameters, returns, overloads and scope. Thirteen rounds, one from every idea in this module. First-try answers earn three stars!

rounds.prompt: Where must your own methods be written?
options: Inside the class, beside main but not inside it
Inside main, above the code that calls them
Outside the class, below the closing brace
rounds.explain: Methods are siblings of `main`. One written inside `main` gives `illegal start of expression`.

rounds.prompt: In what order do these four lines appear?
rounds.explain: A call is a detour: Java runs the whole method, then comes back to the line right after the call.

rounds.prompt: This line will not compile. What is wrong with it?
options: The round brackets are missing, so it is not a call
It needs the word static in front
A method name cannot start with a lower-case letter
rounds.explain: The error is `not a statement`. The brackets are what make a call, even when there is nothing to put in them.

rounds.prompt: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
options: The parameter is the slot declared in the method, the argument is the value passed in
An argument has a type, a parameter does not
They are two words for the same thing
Parameters are for numbers, arguments are for text
rounds.explain: `static void printStars(int count)` declares the parameter. `printStars(7)` supplies the argument.
The method worked on a copy. Changing a parameter never touches the caller's variable, which is why a method that works something out must return it.

rounds.prompt: How do you give a method an optional argument in Java?
options: You cannot: write a shorter overload that fills in the default and calls the longer one
Write `int count = 3` in the parameter list
Pass null and check for it inside
rounds.explain: Java has no default parameter values. Only the long overload should hold the real logic.

rounds.prompt: What does this method hand back for grade(62)?
rounds.explain: The first `return` reached ends the method at once, so nothing below it runs. That is why early returns need no `else`.

options: An age of 60 or more reaches the end of the method with nothing returned
String is not allowed as a return type
There are two returns in one method
The chain needs a switch instead
rounds.explain: Java insists every possible route out of the method hands back a value. Add a final `else` or a `return` after the chain.

rounds.prompt: What is the tidier way to write this?
options: It is already as short as it can be
rounds.explain: The comparison is already true or false, so it can be returned directly. Four lines become one.

rounds.prompt: Given `int half(int n)` and `double half(double n)`, both returning n / 2, what does `half(9)` give?
options: It does not compile: the call is ambiguous
rounds.explain: The type you write picks the overload. 9 is an int, so whole-number division chops the half off; 9.0 goes to the double version.

rounds.prompt: This method is called three times in a row. What does it print?
rounds.explain: A local variable is created fresh on every call and destroyed when the method ends, so it cannot remember anything between calls.

rounds.prompt: Match each piece of method vocabulary to what it means.

pairs.right: Hands nothing back to the caller
A variable that receives a value from the call
Hands a value back and ends the method
The name plus the parameter list
The region where a variable exists

rounds.explain: Six words that describe the whole module. Being able to name these makes every Java error message easier to read.

rounds.prompt: Write a method that returns true only when a score is a valid 0 to 100, and use it.
rounds.explain: A boolean method named as a question. `&&` combines the two halves of the range, and the comparison is returned directly rather than wrapped in an if.
